object.description: Understanding the structure of sequenced genomics-library fragments is essential for accurate read preprocessing. The impact of package selection and versioning on single-cell RNA-seq analysis
object.description: Standard single-cell RNA-seq workflows rely heavily on Seurat and Scanpy for filtering, dimensionality reduction, clustering, and differential expression. Although the packages are thought to implement similar steps, they produce substantially different outputs. Package differences are comparable to analyzing under 5% of reads or under 20% of cells, while version changes also produce substantial differences that are especially pronounced in differential expression.

relations.statement: This publication contains this grounded claim.

evidence.span:
Specifically, there were a handful of cases (4,109 out of
135,185 markers) where Scanpy predicted a logFC near ±30 for a gene in a cluster while
Seurat predicted a logFC near 0.

Universal preprocessing of single-cell genomics data
object.description: Large single-cell atlases depend on comparing datasets generated by many assays, so preprocessing must be consistent before biological interpretation begins. Existing workflows are often assay-specific, while read structures, barcode correction, and UMI/read counting differ across RNA, ATAC, protein, tags, and spatial modalities. cellatlas uses machine-readable seqspec files to configure modular tools for uniform preprocessing across nine datasets, modalities, and single-cell technologies.

relations.statement: This publication contains this grounded claim.

evidence.span: Uniform preprocessing makes it straightforward to compare modalities within the same technology. Figure 2 shows a comparison of data from three different DOGMA-seq (Mimitou et al. 2021) modalities as assayed in (Z. Xu et al. 2022), all preprocessed with cellatlas and the tools it uses: snATAK, kallisto bustools, and kITE. Uniform preprocessing also allows for quantifying the efficiency of assaying the different modalities. The fact that the RNA and protein libraries have a similar number of UMIs captured for a given number of reads (Figure 2a,b) is consistent with similar dilutions of the libraries (1.99nM and 2.2nM respectively), whereas the tag library efficiency (Figure 2c) is distinctly different, likely as a result of dilution to 0.27nM. While the exact cause for the difference requires further investigation, the control for preprocessing that cellatlas provides points to an experimental cause for the difference. Uniform preprocessing also provides a direct comparison of the distinct modalities in terms of their detection efficiency (Figures 2d,e,f). The protein detection saturates because DOGMA-seq protein modality only assayed 163 proteins. The discrepancy between cells in which protein is detected but not ATAC peaks, versus those in which protein is detected but not RNA, is interesting and warrants further investigation.

object.label: Cathryn René Cadwell
A multimodal cell census and atlas of the mammalian primary motor cortex
object.description: Discovering and mapping brain cell types is necessary for understanding brain architecture, development, function, and disease. Rigorous quantitative neuron-type definitions have remained elusive because neurons are locally and projectionally heterogeneous. An integrated mouse, marmoset, and human primary-motor-cortex atlas connected molecular taxonomies with spatial, morphological, physiological, connectivity, developmental, and regulatory features while identifying a conserved hierarchical transcriptomic taxonomy.

object.label: Hannah S. Indralingam
Deciphering the impact of genomic variation on function
object.description: Genomic variation can reveal mechanisms of human biology and genetic predisposition to disease. Understanding how variants alter genome function and phenotype remains challenging without a systematic catalogue of their effects. IGVF combines single-cell mapping, genomic perturbation, and predictive modeling across hundreds of cell types and states, integrating the resulting data, predictions, standards, and pipelines into an open resource.

relations.statement: Hannah S. Indralingam is an author of Deciphering the impact of genomic variation on function.

object.label: The impact of genomic variation on function (IGVF) consortium
object.description: Human genomic variation influences molecular and cellular functions as well as disease-related phenotypes. Understanding how variation alters genome function remains challenging, and interpreting genomic variation requires a systematic catalog of genome function and molecular and cellular variant effects. The IGVF Consortium brings together more than 120 laboratories to integrate single-cell mapping, systematic perturbation, predictive modeling, and a preliminary variant-effect map spanning gene expression, protein activity, and molecular networks.

relations.statement: Hannah S. Indralingam is an author of The impact of genomic variation on function (IGVF) consortium.

object.label: Normalization for sampled count data
object.description: Genomics count normalization should stabilize technical variance, account for depth, and preserve within-cell abundance order. Common proportional-fitting and log workflows can retain depth dependence and conflate scaling with pseudocount choice. PFlog separates pseudocount choice from centered-log-ratio geometry, uniquely satisfies the three normalization desiderata, and outperformed alternatives across hundreds of single-cell RNA-seq datasets.

object.label: Quantifying orthogonal barcodes for sequence census assays
object.description: Barcode-based sequence census assays can label biological features, but barcode design and technical noise complicate quantification. object.label: Assessing the multimodal tradeoff
object.description: Multimodal assays can register chromatin accessibility and gene expression in the same cells, simplifying connections between the two measurements. Assessing tradeoffs across technologies requires uniform processing because distinct assay read structures complicate cross-platform comparisons. snATAK produces results concordant with Cell Ranger while running much faster, and its uniform processing identifies technology-choice tradeoffs in multimodal single-nucleus genomics.

object.label: A machine-readable specification for genomics assays
object.description: Accurate preprocessing of genomics reads depends on knowing how biological and technical sequences are arranged in each library. Assay-specific scripts, divergent parameters, absent sequence annotations, and non-machine-readable library descriptions make uniform processing, comparison, and reanalysis difficult. Seqspec provides a YAML-based library specification and command-line tool that validates assay descriptions and generates technology strings for preprocessing tools.

relations.statement: Assessing the multimodal tradeoff cites A machine-readable specification for genomics assays.

object.label: Metadata retrieval from sequence databases with ffq
object.description: Public sequencing data are increasingly reused with new experiments, making metadata collation and raw-data acquisition essential. Existing metadata tools cover a limited set of databases, while user-uploaded sequencing metadata have little standardization. Ffq exploits shared database hierarchies to retrieve accession- or DOI-associated metadata and raw-data links as JSON and can extend to genomic databases with programmatic access.

object.label: Modular, efficient and constant-memory single-cell RNA-seq preprocessing
object.description: Single-cell RNA-seq preprocessing quantifies transcript or gene abundance in individual cells. Experiments can span 10^6 to 10^10 reads, while existing workflows can require extensive time and disk space or memory that grows with dataset size. kallisto-bustools achieves near-optimal speed, constant memory, scaling to arbitrarily large datasets, Cell Ranger-consistent downstream analyses, and fast RNA-velocity analysis.

relations.statement: This publication is cited in support of this claim.

evidence.span: After read cataloging and error correction, the final step in universal preprocessing is read counting. To quantify the number of features per cell in single-cell genomics assays, molecular counting approaches must be applied in a manner that balances accuracy, speed, and memory while being consistent between assays that do, and do not, have UMIs. We leverage the kallisto bustools counting approach as it performs UMI and read counting in a consistent way. This means that UMIs quantified in scRNAseq data are resolved in a manner that is consistent with reads quantification for scATAC-seq data (Sina Booeshaghi, Gao, and Pachter 2023).

object.label: Seqspec, kallisto-bustools, kITE, and snATAK can in principle preprocess any single-cell genomics assay.
object.description: This publication is cited in support of this claim.

relations.statement: This publication is cited in support of this claim.

evidence.span: The physical-isolation and molecular-capture methods used for an assay are reflected in the structure of reads produced by these methods (Figure 1). The seqspec assay specification (Booeshaghi, Chen, and Pachter 2023) provides a machine-readable format for describing this structure, thereby translating the organizational themes of single-cell genomics into a medium that can, in principle, facilitate automatic and universal preprocessing of single-cell genomics data. While several tools have been developed for preprocessing data from different single-cell RNA-seq assays (He et al. 2022; Battenberg et al. 2022; Melsted et al. 2021), we demonstrate that seqspec (Booeshaghi, Chen, and Pachter 2023), along with kallisto bustools (Melsted et al. 2021), kITE (Sina Booeshaghi et al. 2022) and snATAK (Sina Booeshaghi, Gao, and Pachter 2023), can in principle be used for preprocessing data from any single-cell genomics assay.
